analysis.one_liner: Blocks medical bills from hitting credit reports for 180 days and erases paid-off medical debt from reports.
analysis.headline: The Medical Debt Relief Act, introduced in August 2018 with 7 Democratic sponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Republican-chaired Senate Banking Committee before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required a 180-day waiting period before a medical bill could be placed on a person's credit report, giving people time to resolve insurance disputes or apply for financial aid first. It would have erased medical debts from credit reports within 45 days of being paid or settled. It also would have required debt collectors to send written notice — including the exact date reporting could begin — before putting a medical bill on a credit report.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Americans who carry medical bills. Under the bill, an unexpected hospital bill could not immediately damage their credit score while they waited on insurers or hospital charity programs; once a bill was paid or settled, it would disappear from their report within about 45 days. Cleaner credit reports mean better access to mortgages, car loans, and lower interest rates.

how_it_helps.text: Bars a credit reporting agency from including medical debt information on a report until 180 days have passed since the debt was placed for collection [S3].
Removes fully paid or settled medical debt from credit reports 45 days after payment or settlement, instead of letting it linger for years [S3].

Requires the bill's furnisher to send the consumer a written notice before reporting, stating the specific date the 180-day waiting period ends and explaining the person may use that window to work with insurers or apply for financial assistance [S3].
No one may communicate with or report information to a credit reporting agency about the medical debt during that 180-day period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies and debt collectors that profit from reporting and pursuing medical debt would lose data to sell and collection leverage. Lenders would receive somewhat less information about unpaid medical obligations when making loans. Health care providers that relied on credit reporting to pressure patients into paying would lose one collection tool.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would lose visibility into unpaid medical obligations during the 180-day window, which raises the risk they price into loans for all borrowers [S3].

The bill would not reduce what anyone owes: medical bills would still exist and could still be reported after 180 days and pursued by collectors; it changes only when and whether they appear on credit reports [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is significant and targeted: medical debt is unusual among debts because it often reflects a billing or insurance dispute rather than financial irresponsibility, and the waiting period is designed to let the system resolve those disputes before a credit score is damaged. The cost side is real but modest — lenders lose some information, and collection firms face notice requirements — and the bill preserves collection activity itself, only delaying credit reporting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee — chaired by a Republican — took no further action on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2018 on August 16, 2018, joined by six Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs that same day [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill's action history ends with the referral [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died with it, never having been reported out of committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies, debt collectors, and health care providers that use credit reporting as a collection tool were better off, since the rules limiting medical debt reporting never took effect.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee took no action on the bill during the two years it could have.

industries.note: Agencies sell credit reports and scores, and medical debt has been a large volume of reportable data; the bill would remove new medical debt from reports for 180 days and delete paid ones after 45 days, shrinking their data and the information gap their scores monetize.

The bill requires advance written notice with a specific reporting date and bars reporting for 180 days, removing much of the leverage collectors gain from threatening a patient's credit score; collection activity itself would remain legal [S3].

Providers lose credit reporting as a tool to pressure patients into paying, but patients gain time to settle with insurers or apply for hospital financial assistance, and providers collecting via settlement rather than collections benefit from the 45-day deletion of paid debts.
